name: Posture / frame / body language
lead: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, 'posture', 'frame' and 'body language' describe how a person holds and moves their body. Practitioners use an upright spine, a head stacked over the shoulders, open shoulders and unhurried movement to look taller, broader through the upper body, more athletic and more self-assured, because the alignment of head, shoulders and spine changes the silhouette other people see and the confidence it signals.[8][9]

Posture work is one of the lowest-cost items on the ascension menu: it needs no products or procedures, and members describe it as a 'multiplier' that changes how the same face and body read in photos, in profile and in person.[9] It is usually paired with neck and upper-back training, mobility work, and tongue posture (mewing), which some members treat as part of one chain from tongue to skull to spine.[6][22][25]

Three bodies of work surround the topic. Social psychologists have studied whether adopting expansive or confident postures changes how people feel and how others judge them, most famously in the 'power pose' research of Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap (2010) and the long replication debate that followed.[1][2][12] Physiotherapy researchers have studied corrective exercise for forward head posture, rounded shoulders and thoracic kyphosis and measure results with angles such as the craniovertebral angle.[4][5][11] Nonverbal-communication scholars study how stance, gesture and gaze are read by observers.[13]

angle.text: Upright alignment changes how tall and broad a person appears and how confident they come across. Community members pair posture work with back and neck training so the position becomes the resting default.

paras: 'Posture' refers to the position of the head, spine, shoulders and pelvis at rest and in motion. 'Frame' is community shorthand for the overall impression a body gives: shoulder width, carriage, stillness and presence. 'Body language' covers the gestures, stance, gaze and movement that observers read as confidence, interest or indifference.[13]

Looksmaxxing forum users describe posture as foundational for the face and body, arguing that identical features look different depending on head position and spinal alignment.[8][9] One widely read thread frames the skull as a lever whose orientation depends on posture, and attributes forward head position to overactive upper trapezius muscles and weak lower trapezius and back muscles.[8] Other threads ask for practical cues and exercises, including from members whose abdomen protrudes at rest and who want to correct it.[2][7][21]

Practitioners point to several visual effects. Standing tall adds apparent height, drawing the shoulders back and down widens the upper body, and bringing the head back over the shoulders changes the look of the neck, jawline and facial profile. Some members also report a change in how the face projects in side view when forward head posture is corrected, and some debate whether it makes a recessed face look more or less recessed.[8][10]

In clinical terms, forward head posture is described as a position in which the ear sits in front of a vertical line through the shoulder, often together with rounded shoulders; the combination is called upper crossed syndrome.[11] Physiotherapy research measures head position with the craniovertebral angle and shoulder position with scapular and rounded-shoulder measures, which are the clinical counterparts of what forums call posture fixing.[3][4][5]

Thoracic kyphosis, the forward curve of the upper back, is another visible component. Reference sources describe a typical thoracic curve of roughly 20 to 45 degrees, describe postural kyphosis as the mild, common form associated with slouching, and distinguish it from Scheuermann's kyphosis, which involves structural changes in the vertebrae and cannot be consciously corrected.[14] Postural kyphosis in the young is described as reversible by correcting muscle imbalances.[14]

sections.h: Frame and body language in attractiveness
paras: Looksmaxxing communities treat body language as part of overall attractiveness alongside features and physique. Threads discuss how to read interest versus indifference from stance and gaze, and how upright, still, expansive movement is perceived as confident.[24] Reference summaries of nonverbal communication describe posture as a cue to emotion and status: expansive, forward postures are associated with dominance and approach, while collapsed postures are associated with submission and avoidance, and head tilt is read as pride or shame.[13]

Nonverbal-communication scholars add caveats. Ray Birdwhistell, founder of kinesics, rejected the term 'body language' because gestures do not decode like words and depend on context, and Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted 7-38-55 percentage rule applies only to communication about feelings and attitudes, according to a reference summary.[13] Cultural norms also differ: gestures and eye contact that signal confidence in one culture can read as rude in another.[13]

Carney, Cuddy and Yap published the original study in Psychological Science in 2010. In 42 participants, holding expansive 'high-power' poses for a short period was reported to raise testosterone, lower cortisol and increase risk tolerance and feelings of power.[1] Cuddy's June 2012 TED talk popularised the idea; by 2017 it had about 47 million views, and her book Presence (December 2015) reached the New York Times advice bestseller list in 2016.[1][12]

Ranehill et al. (2015) ran a larger replication and found an effect on felt power but not on hormones or risk-taking.[1] Simmons and Simonsohn's 2016 p-curve analysis concluded that the published evidence did not show an effect once selective reporting was considered, and Garrison et al. and Deuter et al. (2016) and Smith and Apicella (2017) reported null results on physiological or behavioural outcomes.[1] In September 2016 Carney published a statement saying she no longer believed the effects were real.[1]

A June 2017 special issue edited by Joseph Cesario collected eleven new studies and a meta-analysis; it found that the effects on behaviour did not replicate while a medium-sized effect on felt power remained, leaving open whether that effect reflects an experimental artefact.[1] Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse's 2018 analysis of 55 studies reported evidential value for postural-feedback effects, particularly on emotion and affect.[1] Korner et al.'s 2022 review of 128 studies found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, no effect on physiological measures and unclear effects on behaviour, and noted that few studies include a neutral-posture control, so it is unclear whether benefit comes from expansive poses or harm from slumped ones.[1]

Brinol, Petty and Wagner (2009) had participants write positive self-qualities while sitting in a confident or a doubtful posture and found that confident posture strengthened the influence of what they wrote on self-evaluation.[2] Riskind and Gotay (1982) reported more stress in people holding hunched postures, and Oosterwijk et al. (2009) found that priming disappointment made people more likely to lower their height or slump.[2]

Ridley and Asbury (1988) reported that counsellors using an open posture were rated as more capable of giving guidance, and Peper et al. (2018) reported better maths test scores with an erect posture, possibly by reducing stress.[2] Rossberg-Gempton and Poole (1993) linked closed postures with unpleasant feelings.[2] Many entries in this literature lack neutral baselines, and the reference source notes that popular readings of crossed arms and legs have little systematic support.[2]

A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with 627 participants found that corrective exercise produced large changes in craniovertebral angle in people with forward head posture and improved pain, without a clear change in cranial angle.[5] A 2024 meta-analysis of therapeutic exercises for upper crossed syndrome, covering 22 studies, examined forward head posture, rounded shoulders and hyperkyphosis together.[4]

Individual randomised trials have tested a head postural correction program on craniovertebral angle, scapular position and grip strength (2024), scapular stabilisation exercises in women with upper crossed syndrome (2021), and upper thoracic versus upper cervical mobilisation and exercise in people with forward head posture (2017).[16][17][18] A trial of adding a smartphone app to global postural re-education examined neck pain, posture and endurance in people with non-specific neck pain.[19] A review of non-structural sagittal-plane misalignments describes how common postural patterns are classified.[15]

A 2019 review of forward head posture and neck pain reported a significant association in adults with neck pain but not in adolescents.[3] Reference sources attribute forward head posture to prolonged device and desk use and describe combined treatment of strengthening the mid and lower back and deep neck flexors, stretching the upper trapezius, mobilising the thoracic spine and adjusting ergonomics; they also note that popular figures such as the load on the neck per inch of forward head position rest on limited sources.[11]

Forum guides typically combine a few elements: awareness cues for the head, shoulders and pelvis during standing and sitting; strengthening for the upper back and deep neck muscles; mobility work for the chest and thoracic spine; and ergonomic changes to the desk and screen.[8][20][21] Members describe tongue posture as part of the same system, and some claim mewing corrects head alignment, a claim others contest in the same threads.[22][25]

Outside looksmaxxing, programmers and office workers hold similar discussions. Hacker News threads on 'computer guy posture' (2012), an 'epidemic of bad posture' (2016) and putting mirrors around a desk to improve posture (2023) show the same mix of exercise, ergonomics and self-monitoring tips.[26][27][28]

Posture practices are low in risk compared with surgical or pharmacological routes. Clinical sources note that persistent neck, upper-back or shoulder pain, structural curves such as Scheuermann's kyphosis or scoliosis, and rapid changes in posture warrant assessment by a clinician, who may use imaging and measures such as the Cobb angle.[14] Reference summaries state that surgery for severe kyphosis carries complication and reoperation rates in the range of about 5 percent, with some authors suggesting higher.[14]

Reviews of nonverbal behaviour caution that body-language readings are probabilistic and context-dependent, and that claims such as reliable lie detection from posture are not supported by research.[13]

Studies of posture and mood exist, and power-posing trials are summarised above.[1][2] Exercise trials and meta-analyses have measured changes in forward head posture, rounded shoulders and kyphosis.[4][5][16][17][18] No studies were found testing 'frame' as looksmaxxing communities define it, or measuring attractiveness ratings before and after posture correction.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org posture is discussed as a foundational, low-cost way to improve appearance, frequently tied to jaw, neck and tongue position.[6][8][9][22]

claims.claim: Forward head posture held for years changes how the face and skull look
claims.believers: Proponents argue the head acts as a lever and that decades of forward position shape the neck and facial profile.[8]
claims.experts: Physiotherapy reviews document forward head posture and exercise-driven changes in head angle, but studies of facial appearance have not been reported in these reviews.[3][5]

claims.claim: Posture is an overlooked multiplier for the face and frame
claims.believers: Forum authors say upright alignment makes the same features look better and adds apparent height and shoulder width.[9]
claims.experts: No published trial has measured attractiveness ratings before and after posture correction; posture-psychology studies report effects on self-evaluation and observer ratings of competence.[2]

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture can make a recessed face look more recessed
claims.believers: One thread argues that pulling the head back exposes underlying facial recession.[10]
claims.experts: No clinical study has examined this.

claims.claim: Power posing boosts confidence and testosterone
claims.believers: Popularised by a 2012 TED talk and picked up in self-improvement circles.[1][12]
claims.experts: Replications support a felt-power effect but not hormonal changes, and the original first author has said she no longer believes the physiological effects.[1]

claims.claim: Tongue posture (mewing) corrects spinal and head alignment
claims.believers: Some members say the resting tongue position pulls the head back into line and improves posture.[22][25]
claims.experts: Other members in the same threads dispute the mechanism,[8] and the exercise trials reviewed here tested exercise and mobilisation, not tongue position.[4][5]

claims.claim: Corrective exercise can change head and shoulder position
claims.believers: Members share routines for the upper back, deep neck muscles and chest mobility and report improved carriage.[20][21]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of randomised trials report changes in craniovertebral angle and pain after therapeutic exercise in people with forward head posture.[4][5]

claims.claim: Body language alone signals interest or indifference reliably
claims.believers: Dating-oriented threads describe posture and gaze patterns as readable signs of interest.[24]
claims.experts: Nonverbal-communication scholars stress that cues are context- and culture-dependent and not absolute.[13]

card.summary: Open, upright body language to look and feel more confident; feelings effects hold up, hormone and behavior claims do not replicate well.

quick.overview:
Posture and body language practices aim to project confidence through upright, open and expansive stances.

Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel, but the hormonal and behavioral effects reported in 2010 have not replicated well.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is postural feedback: body position influencing mood and self-evaluation.
quick.risks: No direct risks reported. Ongoing disagreement exists about effect sizes.
